A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SciCoQA by the same authors. Their complete text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material across the reorganized appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 21 LLMs, code-only ablations, human validation of predicted discrepancies, and quantitative dataset analyses.

after.justification: V2 reports original evaluations of 22 LLMs, expanded human validation, and additional analyses of judges, reference descriptions, pooled results, and context effects.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 changes final discrepancy validation and rephrasing from GPT-5 alone to GPT-5 plus Gemini 3.1 Pro, with manual verification of disagreements. This revises one data-construction component; the synthetic generation and discrepancy-prediction procedures and substantive prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Human validation in Section 5.2 expands from NLP papers to NLP and CV papers. This broadens coverage specifically within that analysis. The main benchmark retains its scientific domains, programming languages, discrepancy types, and paper-code alignment task.

E2.justification: The main evaluation adds Gemini 3.1 Pro, increasing the lineup from 21 to 22 models. The reported code-only comparison replaces GPT-5 Nano with Gemini 3.1 Pro. More substantially, pooled-ground-truth comparisons, previously reported for three models, now additionally cover all 22 models in v2 Table 6.

E3.justification: V2 accepts matches against either reference description where two exist, changing the main evaluation rule. Dataset composition changes from 81 real and 530 synthetic discrepancies to 92 and 543, including 13 targeted synthetic paper omissions. Human validation expands from 12 papers and 135 predictions to 20 papers and 224 evaluations; the pooled reference set grows from 67 to 129 discrepancies.

E4.justification: V2 adds an alternative Qwen3 32B judge check, reference-description agreement and provider-bias analyses, a relevant-file-position analysis addressing truncation, and a correlation analysis excluding the GPT-5 family. It also expands human error analysis and pooled evaluation. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's existing code-only, language, and synthetic-code analyses.

E5.justification: V2 adds Cohen's kappa estimates for agreement between judges and between evaluations using alternative reference descriptions (Section 4 and Appendix B.1). The existing fixed-seed, five-run mean and standard-deviation reporting remains unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is reported.

E6.justification: The main result tables change substantially: GPT-5's real-data recall is 45.7% in v1 Table 5 and 41.3% in v2 Table 9, while GPT-5 Mini and newly evaluated Gemini 3.1 Pro lead v2 at 46.7%. Changed samples and matching rules prevent interpreting these shifts as controlled performance gains or losses. New agreement, bias, truncation, and pooled-result entries considerably expand the reported evidence.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical propositions or proofs. The discrepancy definition and taxonomy remain substantively unchanged. Additional agreement statistics and alternative descriptions of existing mathematical examples do not introduce new formal reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace the headline finding that GPT-5 leads at 45.7% with Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5 Mini leading at 46.7%. The central contributions—the benchmark, synthetic construction pipeline, and finding of insufficient model recall—remain the same.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about GPT-5's synthetic-data advantage and the advantage enjoyed by models contributing to pooled ground truth. It recommends real data for absolute performance assessment and explains unsuccessful efforts to collect non-CS real examples. New analyses also support interpretations concerning reference-provider bias and long-context difficulty versus truncation.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents exclusion of files larger than 1 MB, specifies Gemini 3.1 Pro's model identifier and metadata, and explains a non-CS generation-prompt adaptation. These improve implementation disclosure; the PDFs do not establish that the newly described file-size filter was absent from v1's actual processing. Hardware, decoding settings, and code/data access information are largely retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations supporting science automation, long-context limitations, incomplete pooled judgments, and verification-oriented peer review, including Boiko, Levy, Buckley and Voorhees, and You. The existing related-work categories and central positioning remain intact. Bibliographic updates to retained works are not new research relationships.

P1.justification: The appendices undergo substantial reorganization: implementation information is consolidated in A, analyses and results are grouped in B and C, examples move to D and E, and prompts move from B to the final Appendix F. Main-text prose receives smaller edits, while limitations and evaluation explanations expand.

P2.justification: V2 adds the reference-comparison Figure 7 and Tables 5–8, revises the correlation plot with a second fit, and expands real examples to display both providers' descriptions. The error table moves into the appendix and gains categories. Prompt boxes are redesigned across full-width pages, substantially changing appendix presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for benchmark validity through second-provider verification with manual adjudication, explicit judge/reference-bias checks, and broader pooled validation. These address v1's dependence on GPT-5-generated references and narrow precision assessment; new synthetic-data and pooling limitations also improve interpretation. Local reporting defects temper the gain—for example, Appendix C.3 gives Gemini 3.1 Pro's final-bin recall as 31.3%, whereas Table 8 reports 37.3%—but do not outweigh the stronger validation.
